items.title: A GenAI lead swapped the LLM-judge in his RAG pipeline for a 33ms verdict model
items.summary: Kameshwara Pavan Kumar Mantha breaks a RAG answer into individual claims, then checks each one against the retrieved evidence with Laya -- a small, non-autoregressive decision model from Convai Innovations -- instead of a second LLM call. Claim-level verdicts land in roughly 33ms, and the pipeline releases, filters, or abstains based on the result.
items.why: This is a live demo of a cheap, fast building block for catching an unsupported RAG claim before it reaches a user, without bolting on another expensive LLM call to judge the first one.
items.action: If any of your RAG or agent pipelines lean on an LLM as judge or reranker, try swapping one narrow check -- like 'does this claim match the retrieved doc?' -- for a small classifier like Laya and see what it does to latency and cost.

eval.reason: A concrete, working alternative to LLM-as-judge for claim verification, with real latency numbers, not a generic RAG tips post.

items.title: Simon Willison: every paid API and cloud service needs a hard budget cap by default
items.summary: Willison argues soft caps -- email me after $X -- aren't enough once coding agents make it trivial to stand up services that quietly rack up usage. He wants a real default: hit the limit, get errors, nothing more, with living dangerously as an explicit opt-in. He points to AWS's new project spending limits and Google Cloud's Spend Caps as the industry finally moving this way.
items.why: Every agent or side project wired up to a paid API is one runaway loop away from a bill you didn't see coming, and most providers still only warn you after the fact.
items.action: Check the APIs behind your own side projects for a real hard spend limit rather than just a billing alert, and turn it on wherever one exists.

eval.reason: A clear, debated position backed by concrete recent product moves (AWS, Google Cloud), not a hot take alone.

items.title: Matt Pocock's Skills plugin v1.3 adds /pr, /implement-spec, and /retro
items.summary: Pocock walks through three new skills in his widely-used Claude Code skills plugin: /implement-spec for landing large chunks of spec'd work, /pr for sharper code review, and /retro for surfacing hidden inefficiencies in past agent sessions.
items.why: These are exactly the three gaps -- speccing big changes, reviewing what the agent wrote, and learning from past sessions -- that make agentic coding feel undisciplined in daily practice.
items.action: 14:34 -- if you're already running Claude Code skills, this is the fastest way to judge whether /implement-spec and /retro are worth adding to your own setup.

items.title: Agents that write their own tools at runtime -- AWS's Sandhya Subramani demos meta-tooling
items.summary: Subramani starts an agent with zero tools, then has it write and load a calculator and a character-counter tool for itself mid-session using the open-source Strands Agents SDK, before moving into self-assembling multi-agent swarms and the guardrails -- sandboxing, permissions, evals -- that keeping that safe actually requires.
items.why: An agent that can write and load its own tool mid-conversation turns the question from 'did I give it the right tools' into 'how do I keep it honest about the ones it invents.'
items.action: 20:40 -- the back half on guardrails and evals for self-modifying agents is the part worth your attention if you're building anything agentic at work.

eval.reason: A concrete, demoed pattern (runtime tool synthesis) plus a real discussion of the safety tradeoffs, not a generic agents talk.
